edges: Luther’s attack on the Lenten oil is a thread in the Reformation’s break with Rome.
The belief that butter caused leprosy and the carnival–Lent allegory are two expressions of the north–south fat divide in the same centuries.
Khosrova notes that the dairy-rich butter-eating nations were largely those that broke from Rome, the Dutch among them.
Khosrova links the Lenten allowance of butter in the north to its spread south and its rise as a status symbol in Italy.
The Basque voyages to Labrador are part of the Atlantic expansion that Ellis describes.
Basque harpooners were hired on the first English and Dutch voyages to Spitsbergen.
The Muscovy Company’s monopoly and charter set up the English side of the Spitsbergen fishery.
Ellis shows the English and Dutch arming their whalers over Spitsbergen from 1613.
The Navigation Act of 1651 was meant to restrict Dutch whale oil, in the war’s background.
The warm decade of 1625–35 made shore whaling harder, as Ellis relates.
Merchants and soap-boilers financing a whaling voyage are the English market that Spitsbergen oil served.
Soap-boilers are the trade London’s 1618 order regulated and the one that invested in whale oil at Leith.
Houghton’s account of tallow, candles and soap describes the London trades that the 1618 order regulated.
The Atlantic trade of the 1600s is the setting in which palm oil moves from Angola to Brazil.
Zuckerman ties the palm-oil exchange to the slave ships’ provisions and the boiling of the fruit by women captives.
Missionaries and settlers carry olive oil and then olive trees across the Atlantic.
Britain’s hope for sesame oil as a substitute for olive oil answers the colonial oil trade of the Spanish.
Song Yingxing’s ranking of oils and his description of the press come from the same chapter of the Tiangong kaiwu.
The Guinea coast’s own uses of palm oil are the market that Portuguese and Atlantic traders entered.
The Cape’s whales went unhunted because the Dutch company already had oil and baleen from Spitsbergen.
Java’s oil in place of butter is the Far Eastern side of the butter-against-oil quarrel that Europe fights in the Lenten fat line.
Southeast Asia’s lamp oils and London’s tallow candles are two answers to the same demand for evening light.
Edo Japan’s rapeseed lamps and Southeast Asia’s kemiri-nut lamps are the same lamp-oil move on two coasts of Asia.
Tempura’s frying oil and the rapeseed lamp are two uses of the oil that Edo Japan began to produce.
The peanut’s arrival and Song Yingxing’s ranking of the oils belong to the same Ming-Qing oil economy.
Vijayanagara’s sesame oil and the American South’s benne are the same Indian oilseed on two continents.
Bengal’s ghee exports and Italy’s butter fashion are two stories of a dairy fat entering trade.
Taiji’s five crews and the Dutch Spitsbergen fleet began within years of each other, a world apart.
The Spanish carry the pig and the olive across the Atlantic together: the fat of the forest and the fat of the south.
Cacao fat in Central America and olive oil shipped to Spanish America are two fats meeting in the same colonial kitchens, one native and one imported.
Avocado and cacao are the two distinctively Mesoamerican fats this folio can document, one a structural staple and one a surprising substitute for lard.
Landa’s Yucatec account and Oviedo’s Nicaraguan anecdote are two independent sixteenth-century reports of the same Mesoamerican practice: rendering cacao into a butter-like fat.

Ethiopia’s Lenten ban on butter and Luther’s attack on Rome’s Lenten butter dispensations are mirror-image fasting economies of the same century, one forbidding the fat Rome was selling the right to eat.
The Agaw’s butter caravans to Gondar and the same country’s Lenten butter ban and butter-soaked court cuisine are the production and consumption ends of one Ethiopian fat economy.
